fp1_polar_coordinates.description: Convert between Cartesian and polar coordinates, recognise circle and line equations, and retain the specified branch.

sections.title: How do polar coordinates give horizontal and vertical positions?
sections.label: Resolve the radius in two directions
sections.intro: The initial line is the positive x-axis. Measure the given angle from it and project the radius onto the two axes.

blocks.html: \(x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta\) with the radius non-negative for this convention.

blocks.title: Resolve a radius horizontally and vertically
blocks.prompt: Convert polar point \(\left(6,\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\) to Cartesian coordinates. Angles are in radians and the initial line is the positive x-axis.
blocks.hint: Keep the signs of the trigonometric functions, even though the radius is positive.
blocks.solution:
Resolve the radius using \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\).

Use the exact cosine and sine at \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\). Their signs locate the correct quadrant.

This gives Cartesian point \(\left(-3,3 \sqrt{3}\right)\).

blocks.html: Positive radius does not make both Cartesian coordinates positive. Use the signs of the trigonometric factors.

sections.title: How do I find the correct polar angle from a point?
sections.label: Use the original quadrant
sections.intro: Find the radius by Pythagoras. Then use the signs of both Cartesian coordinates to choose an angle in the stated interval.

blocks.html: \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Use both \(\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{y}{r}\) when the quadrant is uncertain.

blocks.title: Use both signs to choose the polar angle
blocks.prompt: Write \(\left(-3,3 \sqrt{3}\right)\) in polar form with \(r>0,\ -\pi<\theta\le\pi\). Give exact radius and angle.
blocks.hint: The value from inverse tangent can lie in a different quadrant. Use both coordinates.
blocks.solution:
The radius is \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), giving \(6\).

Use the signs of x and y to identify the quadrant. Sine and cosine are \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(- \frac{1}{2}\) at the chosen direction.

The polar pair in the stated angle interval is \(\left(6,\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\).

blocks.html: An inverse-tangent calculation alone may return the angle of the opposite ray. Check the signs and range.

sections.title: How does a simple polar rule give a circle?
sections.label: Use a standard Cartesian identity
sections.intro: Multiply an equation involving sine or cosine by r so that the resulting factors can be replaced.

blocks.html: Replace \(r^2\) by \(x^2+y^2\), and \(r\sin\theta\) by \(y\). Complete the square to identify the centre.

figure.caption: The pole lies on the circle. Its centre is above the origin.
figure.alt: The circle has centre (0, 2) and radius two. Its lowest point is the pole, and its highest point is (0, 4).

blocks.title: Complete the square to identify a polar circle
blocks.prompt: For \(r=6 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(0\le\theta\le \pi\), find the centre and radius of the traced circle.
blocks.hint: Use r² and r sin θ to remove the polar variables.
blocks.solution:
Multiply by r to get \(r^2=6r\sin\theta\). Replace these expressions to get \(x^{2} + y^{2} - 6 y=0\).

Completing the square gives \(x^{2} + \left(y - 3\right)^{2}=9\).

The centre is \(\left(0,3\right)\) and the radius is \(3\). The angle interval traces the complete circle, including the pole.

blocks.html: Include the pole if the radius is zero at an allowed angle. The equation can describe a whole circle or a restricted arc depending on the stated angles.

blocks.title: Complete the square to identify a polar circle
blocks.prompt: For \(r=10 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(0\le\theta\le \pi\), find the centre and radius of the traced circle.
blocks.hint: Use r² and r sin θ to remove the polar variables.
blocks.solution:
Multiply by r to get \(r^2=10r\sin\theta\). Replace these expressions to get \(x^{2} + y^{2} - 10 y=0\).

Completing the square gives \(x^{2} + \left(y - 5\right)^{2}=25\).

The centre is \(\left(0,5\right)\) and the radius is \(5\). The angle interval traces the complete circle, including the pole.

sections.title: When does a reciprocal trigonometric radius give a line?
sections.label: Recognise r times the relevant ratio
sections.intro: An equation for r involving secant can be rewritten as a constant horizontal component.

blocks.html: Use \(\sec\theta=\frac1{\cos\theta}\) whenever the cosine is non-zero, then multiply by the cosine.

blocks.title: Convert a polar secant rule without introducing endpoints
blocks.prompt: The polar relation is \(r=3\sec\theta\) for \(-\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Give its Cartesian equation and y-coordinate when \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

fields.label: Cartesian equation in x and y

blocks.hint: Use the definition of Cartesian x rather than squaring the relation.
blocks.solution:
Multiply by cosine. The expression \(r\cos\theta\) is x, giving \(x=3\).

Inside the angle interval r is positive. All real y-values occur as \(y=3\tan\theta\).

At the specified angle the tangent is one, giving \(y=3\).

blocks.html: Record the angles where secant is undefined. Do not add an endpoint simply because it disappears from the new equation.

sections.title: What happens to the angle restriction when I eliminate θ?
sections.label: Supply the Cartesian branch condition
sections.intro: A Cartesian equation can encode several branches of the full relation. Use the given angular interval to select the requested branch.

blocks.html: Convert the double-angle expression using sine and cosine in terms of x and y. Then state any restrictions on x or y that the conversion alone does not retain.

blocks.title: Keep the right-hand loop after eliminating the angle
blocks.prompt: The curve is \(r^2=9\cos(2\theta)\) for \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{4}\). Give the Cartesian equation, and its positive x-intercept.

fields.label: Cartesian equation in x and y

blocks.hint: The algebraic equation can contain a second loop. State the branch restriction with it.
blocks.solution:
For non-pole points, \(\cos(2\theta)=\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}\). Multiply through to obtain \(- 9 x^{2} + 9 y^{2} + \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)^{2}=0\).

The pole also satisfies that equation, but the angle restriction keeps only the loop with \(x\ge0\).

At \(\theta=0\), \(r=3\), so the positive intercept is \(\left(3,0\right)\).

blocks.html: Squaring or clearing powers of the radius can introduce solutions outside the interval. Check the pole as a separate case.

blocks.title: Keep the right-hand loop after eliminating the angle
blocks.prompt: The curve is \(r^2=25\cos(2\theta)\) for \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{4}\). Give the Cartesian equation, and its positive x-intercept.

fp1_polar_sketches.description: Find non-negative radius intervals, symmetry, endpoints and landmarks before tracing a polar curve.

sections.title: Which parts of the radius rule should I draw?
sections.label: Check non-negative radius
sections.intro: Find the permitted angular intervals before plotting. In this course use the non-negative-radius convention.

blocks.html: Where a radius changes sign, split the interval at its zeros. A connected petal can start and end at the pole.

figure.caption: Only the permitted positive-radius petal is drawn.
figure.alt: One petal in the first quadrant starts and ends at the pole. Its farthest point from the pole lies on the diagonal ray.

blocks.title: Find the angular interval for a non-negative petal
blocks.prompt: On \(0\le\theta\le \pi\), keep only non-negative values in \(r=3 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\). Give the complete allowed angle interval in interval notation, containing \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) and the maximum radius.
blocks.hint: Find where 2θ runs through a non-negative sine interval, then divide both endpoints by two.
blocks.solution:
The sine factor is non-negative from zero through \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) in this part of the interval.

The isolated angle \(\pi\) is also a pole, but lies outside the requested connected piece.

Within the requested interval the sine reaches one at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\), so the maximum radius is \(3\).

blocks.html: Do not draw a reflected negative-radius branch in a question that restricts r to non-negative values.

sections.title: Which landmarks establish the shape of a cardioid?
sections.label: Find the zero and farthest points
sections.intro: Use the extreme cosine values and the coordinate axes as starting rays. Evaluate the radius on these rays and place the points.

blocks.html: The largest radius determines the farthest point from the pole. Use its angle to decide which side of the initial line it lies on.

blocks.title: Use the pole and opposite-axis landmark
blocks.prompt: For \(r=3 - 3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) on \(0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\), identify the greatest radius and the x-coordinate of the point attaining it.
blocks.hint: Sketch the point at θ = π before assigning the Cartesian sign.
blocks.solution:
The radius is zero at the two ends, meeting the pole. Reflection across the initial line corresponds to replacing θ by \(2\pi-\theta\).

The largest radius occurs where cosine is minus one, at \(\theta=\pi\). It is \(6\).

At that angle the point lies to the left of the pole on the x-axis. Its x-coordinate is \(-6\).

blocks.html: A radius is a distance. Its value at the negative x-axis has a positive radius but a negative Cartesian x-coordinate.

sections.title: When can I reflect one half of a sketch?
sections.label: Compare opposite angles
sections.intro: Under reflection in the initial line an angle changes to its negative. The radius must be the same on the reflected ray.

blocks.html: If both angles are in the domain and the radius function is even, use reflection to complete the graph.

blocks.title: Use symmetry to complete an admissible lobe
blocks.prompt: For \(r=3 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\) on \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{4}\), find the greatest radius and decide whether the curve is symmetric about the initial line.
blocks.hint: Compare radii at opposite angles in the given angle interval.
blocks.solution:
Cosine is even, so replacing θ by its negative leaves the radius unchanged.

Both endpoints have zero radius. Their intermediate points form one connected lobe reflected across the initial line.

The maximum occurs at \(\theta=0\), when cosine is one. It equals \(3\).

blocks.html: Check the allowed interval too. Symmetry of a formula does not automatically give symmetry of a restricted arc.

blocks.hint: Compare radii at opposite angles in the given angle interval.
blocks.solution:

Both endpoints have zero radius. Their intermediate points form one connected lobe reflected across the initial line.

The maximum occurs at \(\theta=0\), when cosine is one. It equals \(5\).

sections.title: How can an increasing radius determine a spiral?
sections.label: Mark both endpoint rays
sections.intro: When the direction turns and the radius steadily grows, the curve traces an outward spiral segment.

blocks.html: Evaluate positive radius at the start, the end and one intermediate axis. Then attach each point to the correct ray.

blocks.title: Sketch a spiral from its endpoint rays
blocks.prompt: For \(r=2 \theta + 3\) on \(0\le\theta\le \pi\), find the starting x-coordinate, ending x-coordinate and the height on the positive y-axis.
blocks.hint: Evaluate the radius on each special ray and use the direction to give signed coordinates.
blocks.solution:
The radius increases as the direction turns anticlockwise. At θ zero the starting point is \(\left(3,0\right)\).

At θ equal to π, the curve lies on the negative x-axis, so the ending position is \(\left(- 2 \pi - 3,0\right)\).

At \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\) the radius equals the y-coordinate, giving \(3 + \pi\).

blocks.html: The start is not automatically the pole. Calculate its radius at the lower angular limit.

sections.title: How do I distinguish the pole from another point on an axis?
sections.label: Use the radius with each special angle
sections.intro: An axis point can occur because a sine or cosine projection vanishes even when the radius is non-zero.

blocks.html: First find all cases where radius is zero. Then check the permitted axis directions separately for ordinary intercepts.

blocks.title: Distinguish a pole from an ordinary axis crossing
blocks.prompt: The curve is \(r=3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 3\) for \(0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\). Give the positive x-intercept and the angle at the pole.
blocks.hint: Use r = 0 for the pole. Check ordinary axis intersections separately.
blocks.solution:
The initial line is crossed at \(\theta=0\) with radius \(6\). The right intercept is \(\left(6,0\right)\).

A pole point has r equal to zero, requiring cosine minus one.

This occurs at \(\theta=\pi\) within the stated interval.

blocks.html: Several angles may describe the same pole. Do not count the origin as a different point for each such angle.

blocks.solution:

A pole point has r equal to zero, requiring cosine minus one.

This occurs at \(\theta=\pi\) within the stated interval.

sections.title: When does an equality of radii give a common point?
sections.label: Use a common ray and a positive radius

blocks.title: Equate the distances on a common ray
blocks.prompt: Find the polar coordinates in the first quadrant of the common point of \(r=6 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(r=3\).
blocks.hint: Solve on the stated quadrant before evaluating the radius.
blocks.solution:
At a non-pole intersection both curves have the same positive radius along the same ray.

Equating radii gives \(\cos\theta=\frac12\). The first-quadrant solution is \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

The shared radius is \(3\), so the point is \(\left(3,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\).

sections.intro: A zero radius is the same Cartesian point for all angles. For the pole, it is enough that each curve reaches zero somewhere in its own domain.

blocks.title: Check the pole through each curve separately
blocks.prompt: The full non-negative-radius circles are \(r=6 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(r=6 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\). Give the polar radius and angle of their common non-pole point. Do they also share the pole?

fields.label: Does the pole belong to both?

blocks.hint: A shared pole does not require the same angle to give zero radius on both curves.
blocks.solution:
The positive shared radii give cosine equal to sine. Their common positive-angle ray is at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

The shared radius is \(3 \sqrt{2}\).

The cosine circle has zero radius at a y-axis direction. The sine circle has zero radius on the initial line. These both denote the same geometric pole.

blocks.html: Failure to find a simultaneous zero at the same angle does not rule out the shared pole.

fp1_polar_areas.description: Calculate polar sector, petal and overlapping areas. Split active boundaries and account for straight edges.

sections.title: Why does a polar sector use half the square of the radius?
sections.label: Integrate the sector element
sections.intro: A small wedge with angle in radians has area approximately half its radius squared times its angle. Sum wedges over the interval as their widths tend to zero.

blocks.html: \(A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,\mathrm d\theta\) when the boundary is traced once on the interval.

blocks.title: Integrate one petal exactly once
blocks.prompt: Find the exact area of the petal \(r=3 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\) for \(0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\). Give the multiplier of \(\pi\) in the area.
blocks.hint: Use the given one-petal interval in radians.
blocks.solution:
The interval runs from the pole round one petal back to the pole. The sector element is \(\frac12r^2\,\mathrm d\theta\).

Replace \(\sin^2(2\theta)\) with \(\frac12\bigl(1-\cos(4\theta)\bigr)\).

The cosine contribution integrates to zero at these endpoints. The area is \(\frac{9 \pi}{8}\).

blocks.html: Use radians and square the entire radius before integrating. Counting the same petal twice doubles the answer.

sections.title: How is a spiral area measured between two rays?
sections.label: Integrate the changing radius
sections.intro: The two rays determine the angular limits. The curve gives how far the sector extends on each ray.

blocks.html: Substitute the spiral radius, square it, and use the corresponding limits. A non-constant radius cannot be replaced with its final value.

blocks.title: Square the radius before integrating the spiral
blocks.prompt: Find the area between \(r=3 \theta\) and the two endpoint rays on \(0\le\theta\le 3\).
blocks.hint: The integral uses the square of the radius and the factor one half.
blocks.solution:
The radius is non-negative on the interval and sweeps each angle once.

Use \(A=\frac12\int_0^{3}\left(3 \theta\right)^2\,\mathrm d\theta\).

Integrate the squared radius to obtain \(\frac{81}{2}\).

blocks.html: A missing factor of one half or a missing square changes the area’s scale.

sections.label: Split when the smaller radius changes
sections.intro: Each ray in the common region is cut off at the smaller of the two radii. Mark the intersection angles before integrating.

blocks.html: Split the integral at the switch angles and use the smaller radius on each interval. Use symmetry only after identifying what is being reflected.

figure.caption: Use the smaller radius at each angle inside the lens.
figure.alt: Two circles meet at the pole and at (1, 1). The shaded lens in the first quadrant is their common region.

blocks.title: Split the area when the smaller radius changes
blocks.prompt: Find the common area of the two full circles \(r=3 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(r=3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) with non-negative radii. Give coefficients in \(A=p\pi+q\).
blocks.hint: For a common interior use the smaller radius and split at the equal-radius ray.
blocks.solution:
The common interior is in the first quadrant. The sine radius is smaller before \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\), and the cosine radius is smaller after it.

Integrate half the smaller squared radius on each interval. By symmetry both contributions are equal.

Using the sine double-angle identity in the first part gives total \(- \frac{9}{4} + \frac{9 \pi}{8}\).

blocks.html: Using the larger radius instead gives some points that belong to only one region.

blocks.html: \(A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta \left(r_{\rm outer}^2-r_{\rm inner}^2\right)\,\mathrm d\theta\).

blocks.title: Subtract squared radii on a shared angular interval
blocks.prompt: Between the rays \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), find the area inside \(r=5\) and outside \(r=3\). Give the coefficient of \(\pi\).
blocks.hint: The difference of the squares is not the square of the difference.
blocks.solution:
The outer sector has radius \(5\) and the inner sector radius \(3\).

Subtract half the inner radius squared from half the outer radius squared at each angle, then integrate over the common interval.

The area is \(4 \pi\).

blocks.html: The difference of squares is not the square of the difference.

At the chord endpoints \(\sin\theta=\frac12\), so the rays are \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\theta=\frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

The enclosed area equals the sector between these rays minus the triangle from the pole to the chord.

The angle at the pole is \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\). Use the sector and sine-area formulae to get \(- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{4} + 3 \pi\).

extraPractice.solution:
The radius is non-negative on the interval and sweeps each angle once.

Use \(A=\frac12\int_0^{4}\left(4 \theta\right)^2\,\mathrm d\theta\).

Integrate the squared radius to obtain \(\frac{512}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Split the area when the smaller radius changes
extraPractice.prompt: Find the common area of the two full circles \(r=6 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\) and \(r=6 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) with non-negative radii. Give coefficients in \(A=p\pi+q\).
extraPractice.hint: For a common interior use the smaller radius and split at the equal-radius ray.
extraPractice.solution:
The common interior is in the first quadrant. The sine radius is smaller before \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\), and the cosine radius is smaller after it.

Integrate half the smaller squared radius on each interval. By symmetry both contributions are equal.

Using the sine double-angle identity in the first part gives total \(-9 + \frac{9 \pi}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Subtract squared radii on a shared angular interval
extraPractice.prompt: Between the rays \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\), find the area inside \(r=6\) and outside \(r=4\). Give the coefficient of \(\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: The difference of the squares is not the square of the difference.
extraPractice.solution:
The outer sector has radius \(6\) and the inner sector radius \(4\).

Subtract half the inner radius squared from half the outer radius squared at each angle, then integrate over the common interval.

The area is \(5 \pi\).

extraPractice.title: Subtract a triangle for a straight boundary
extraPractice.prompt: Inside \(r=6\), find the area above the chord \(y=3\). Give coefficients in \(A=p\pi+q\sqrt3\).
extraPractice.hint: The sector alone includes the central triangle below the chord.
extraPractice.solution:
At the chord endpoints \(\sin\theta=\frac12\), so the rays are \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\theta=\frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

The enclosed area equals the sector between these rays minus the triangle from the pole to the chord.

The angle at the pole is \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\). Use the sector and sine-area formulae to get \(- 9 \sqrt{3} + 12 \pi\).

fp1_polar_extrema.description: Choose the appropriate distance from the pole or an axis, locate extrema and check tangent directions using coordinate derivatives.

sections.title: When is the quantity to maximise just the radius?
sections.label: Optimise the radial distance directly
sections.intro: For the non-negative-radius convention, the distance from the pole is r. This is not the same as the height from a horizontal line.

blocks.html: Find any stationary radii inside the allowed interval and compare their values with the endpoints and admissible limiting values.

blocks.title: Maximise the distance measured from the pole
blocks.prompt: For \(r=5 - \left(\theta - 1\right)^{2}\) on \(0\le\theta\le 2\), give the greatest distance from the pole and the angle attaining it.
blocks.hint: Use the radius directly only when the distance is measured from the pole.
blocks.solution:
The distance from the pole is the non-negative radius itself.

The subtracted square attains its minimum value zero at \(\theta=1\). This angle is within the domain.

The greatest radius is \(5\). Both endpoint values are lower.

blocks.html: A largest radius can occur at an endpoint. Checking only stationary points can miss it.

sections.title: How do I find the greatest height above the initial line?
sections.label: Optimise the vertical projection
sections.intro: The height above the initial line is y. The perpendicular distance is its magnitude, and in the upper half-plane the two agree.

blocks.html: Use \(y=r\sin\theta\) before taking a derivative or recognising a trigonometric maximum.

figure.caption: Greatest height and greatest radius occur at different points.
figure.alt: The top of the first-quadrant semicircle is at (1, 1), at an angle of π over four. The farthest point from the pole is (2, 0).

blocks.title: Maximise perpendicular distance from the initial line
blocks.prompt: Find the greatest height above the initial line and its angle for \(r=3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) on \(0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\).
blocks.hint: Use the Cartesian vertical coordinate to measure height, not r alone.
blocks.solution:
The height is \(y=r\sin\theta\). Here this gives \(y=\frac{3}{2}\sin(2\theta)\).

The sine reaches one at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\) in the allowed interval.

Therefore the greatest height is \(\frac{3}{2}\), while the endpoint heights are both zero.

blocks.html: Maximising r alone can pick a point on the initial line instead of above it.

sections.title: What makes a tangent horizontal?
sections.label: Check that only the vertical derivative vanishes
sections.intro: Use the Cartesian coordinates as functions of the angle. A regular tangent has a non-zero derivative vector.

blocks.html: For a horizontal tangent the y derivative is zero and the x derivative is non-zero. Substitute into the original coordinates to find its height.

blocks.title: Check the companion derivative at a horizontal tangent
blocks.prompt: For the petal \(r=3 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\) on \(0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\), find the value of \(\sin^2\theta\) for its non-pole horizontal tangent and the height of that tangent.
blocks.hint: A zero y derivative shows a horizontal tangent only if the x derivative is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The height is \(6\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\). Differentiate it with respect to the angle.

The derivative is \(6 \left(2 - 3 \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}\right) \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\). At a non-pole horizontal tangent this vanishes when \(\sin^2\theta=\frac23\).

The x derivative at this angle is \(- 2 \sqrt{3}\), non-zero. Using the positive cosine gives height \(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\).

blocks.html: A zero derivative of r does not by itself give the direction of a Cartesian tangent.

blocks.title: Check the companion derivative at a horizontal tangent
blocks.prompt: For the petal \(r=5 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\) on \(0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\), find the value of \(\sin^2\theta\) for its non-pole horizontal tangent and the height of that tangent.
blocks.hint: A zero y derivative shows a horizontal tangent only if the x derivative is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The height is \(10\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\). Differentiate it with respect to the angle.

The derivative is \(10 \left(2 - 3 \sin^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}\right) \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\). At a non-pole horizontal tangent this vanishes when \(\sin^2\theta=\frac23\).

The x derivative at this angle is \(- \frac{10 \sqrt{3}}{3}\), non-zero. Using the positive cosine gives height \(\frac{20 \sqrt{3}}{9}\).

sections.title: What makes a tangent vertical?
sections.label: Check that only the horizontal derivative vanishes
sections.intro: Interchange the roles of the coordinate derivatives. A vertical line can occur at an interior angle even if r is not extreme there.

blocks.html: For a regular vertical tangent the x derivative is zero and the y derivative is non-zero.

blocks.title: Locate a vertical tangent using the x derivative
blocks.prompt: Find the non-pole vertical tangent of \(r=3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\) on \(- \frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\). Give its x-coordinate and angle.
blocks.hint: Find where the x derivative is zero and confirm that the other derivative is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal coordinate is \(3 \cos^{2}{\left(\theta \right)}\). Its derivative vanishes at angle zero and the two endpoints.

Both endpoints have zero radius so this question excludes them. At zero, the vertical derivative is \(3\), so the curve is regular there.

The point has horizontal coordinate \(3\). The tangent is \(x=3\).

blocks.html: If both coordinate derivatives vanish, analyse the local curve before assigning a tangent direction.

sections.title: How can I find a tangent when the radius is zero?
sections.label: Use the limiting direction
sections.intro: The origin can correspond to several angular endpoints. Consider the curve approaching it from each admissible side.

blocks.html: Use the limiting ray direction or calculate the coordinate derivatives directly. Check whether different branches have different tangent directions.

blocks.title: Find the limiting tangent at the pole
blocks.prompt: The curve \(r=3 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\) starts at the pole at \(\theta=0\). Find the x derivative there and choose the direction of the tangent.
blocks.hint: At the pole, use the limiting directions or the coordinate derivatives if at least one is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The polar radius is zero at the starting point. Compute the coordinate derivatives separately rather than dividing by r.

Here the x derivative at the start is \(3\) and the y derivative is zero.

The tangent is therefore horizontal. The same line follows from the direction of the approaching ray.

blocks.html: Dividing by radius at a pole discards the very point where the tangent is requested.
